A quote in the term ends the literal and the rest of the request becomes SQL — the classic unauthenticated read of any table the storefront role can reach. The ORDER BY fragment genuinely cannot be bound, but the term can be, and the two got composed the same way.

outcomes.architecture: Bun services: `Bun.serve` processes in apps/wallet-api (routes objects, regex dispatch and WebSocket handlers over Bun.sql and bun:sqlite) plus two standalone document/statement services under services/.
outcomes.why: The presented webhook signature is compared to the computed HMAC with `!==`, which short-circuits at the first differing character and so leaks how much of a guessed signature was correct. Because the caller controls the body and can replay the same request indefinitely, that side channel is a path to forging a `payout.settled` event, which is the one thing this endpoint's signature check exists to prevent. A constant-time comparison is required here.

outcomes.architecture: Bun services: `Bun.serve` processes in apps/wallet-api (routes objects, regex dispatch and WebSocket handlers over Bun.sql and bun:sqlite) plus two standalone document/statement services under services/.
outcomes.why: The comparison at line 44 is still `===`, but it operates on two keyed SHA-256 digests taken under a 32-byte nonce generated freshly for this request. The strings that meet the operator are unpredictable to the caller, so where they first differ carries no information about the real signature and the same body replayed twice produces unrelated pairs. This is the standard blinded (double-HMAC) comparison and it is not timing-exploitable.

outcomes.architecture: Bun services: `Bun.serve` processes in apps/wallet-api (routes objects, regex dispatch and WebSocket handlers over Bun.sql and bun:sqlite) plus two standalone document/statement services under services/.

A single quote in `q` closes the literal, so the reporting role's whole search path is reachable - and although that role is read-only, the replica still holds every tenant's transactions.

outcomes.architecture: Bun services: `Bun.serve` processes in apps/wallet-api (routes objects, regex dispatch and WebSocket handlers over Bun.sql and bun:sqlite) plus two standalone document/statement services under services/.

outcomes.architecture: Bun services: `Bun.serve` processes in apps/wallet-api (routes objects, regex dispatch and WebSocket handlers over Bun.sql and bun:sqlite) plus two standalone document/statement services under services/.

outcomes.architecture: Bun services: `Bun.serve` processes in apps/wallet-api (routes objects, regex dispatch and WebSocket handlers over Bun.sql and bun:sqlite) plus two standalone document/statement services under services/.

outcomes.architecture: Deno Fresh app with file-routed handlers under routes/ and a hand-rolled server layer under server/: URLPattern-dispatched handlers over deno-postgres and Deno KV, with the session resolved by routes/_middleware.ts.

outcomes.architecture: Chrome MV3 extension: a background service worker with chrome.runtime onMessage/onMessageExternal listeners, a command router, a chrome.storage.sync settings merger, fetch-based preview handlers, and content scripts that render a panel into a shadow root on every page.
outcomes.why: `onMessageExternal` is the door open to web pages and other extensions, and this listener hands every message straight to the same privileged command table with no check on `sender.origin` or `sender.id` at all - the TODO above it admits `externally_connectable` has not been narrowed either. Any page that can reach the channel can therefore send `session.token` and walk away with the user's sync token, or `session.describe` for their email, or `session.signOut`.

outcomes.architecture: Chrome MV3 extension: a background service worker with chrome.runtime onMessage/onMessageExternal listeners, a command router, a chrome.storage.sync settings merger, fetch-based preview handlers, and content scripts that render a panel into a shadow root on every page.
outcomes.why: The external listener refuses anything that is not a browser-attested trusted sender before dispatching: `sender.id` must be the one companion extension id, or `sender.origin` must be an exact member of the two-entry origin set. Both fields are stamped by the browser rather than taken from the message body, and origin equality cannot be satisfied by a lookalike host or by plain http, so `session.token` is only ever served to the app that is allowed to hold it.

outcomes.architecture: Chrome MV3 extension: a background service worker with chrome.runtime onMessage/onMessageExternal listeners, a command router, a chrome.storage.sync settings merger, fetch-based preview handlers, and content scripts that render a panel into a shadow root on every page.
outcomes.why: `route` resolves the handler out of both tables and calls it without ever consulting `senderKind`, even though it computed it one line earlier and the module's own header says workspace commands are meant to be driven from the options page only. A content script runs in every tab and is one page-controlled `postMessage` bridge away from the site it was injected into, so any visited page can reach the workspace-wide commands. The bare table index also resolves inherited keys such as `constructor`, which is why the sibling router uses `Object.hasOwn`.

outcomes.architecture: Chrome MV3 extension: a background service worker with chrome.runtime onMessage/onMessageExternal listeners, a command router, a chrome.storage.sync settings merger, fetch-based preview handlers, and content scripts that render a panel into a shadow root on every page.
outcomes.why: Workspace commands are only resolved once the sender has been classified as the extension's own page; a content script or an external sender asking for one gets `forbidden` and the handler is never looked up. Lookups also go through `Object.hasOwn`, so a caller-supplied action cannot resolve to an inherited property of the command table.

outcomes.architecture: Chrome MV3 extension: a background service worker with chrome.runtime onMessage/onMessageExternal listeners, a command router, a chrome.storage.sync settings merger, fetch-based preview handlers, and content scripts that render a panel into a shadow root on every page.
outcomes.why: `merge` walks the keys of a JSON document the caller supplied and recurses into `target[key]` with no reserved-key filter. `JSON.parse` produces an own `__proto__` property, so a document shaped like `{"__proto__":{"trusted":true}}` makes the recursion write onto Object.prototype, and every object in the worker inherits the new property. `isTrustedOrigin` a few lines below reads `settings.origins[origin]?.trusted` with no own-property check, so that single patch marks every origin trusted.

outcomes.architecture: Chrome MV3 extension: a background service worker with chrome.runtime onMessage/onMessageExternal listeners, a command router, a chrome.storage.sync settings merger, fetch-based preview handlers, and content scripts that render a panel into a shadow root on every page.
outcomes.why: The merge skips `__proto__`, `constructor` and `prototype` before touching `target`, and it only recurses into an existing subtree when that subtree is an own property, replacing it with a fresh object otherwise - so no assignment can reach Object.prototype. `isTrustedOrigin` additionally requires an own property on `settings.origins`, so an inherited key could not be read as a decision even if one existed.

outcomes.architecture: Chrome MV3 extension: a background service worker with chrome.runtime onMessage/onMessageExternal listeners, a command router, a chrome.storage.sync settings merger, fetch-based preview handlers, and content scripts that render a panel into a shadow root on every page.
outcomes.why: `note.quote`, `note.author` and `note.sourceTitle` are interpolated raw into an HTML template that is then assigned through `innerHTML` at line 57. The notes are not the extension's own strings: they arrive from the background worker via `sendCommand` in ../shared/messaging, having been captured as page text on whatever site a teammate was reading, so a highlight saved from a hostile page carries markup into every teammate's tab. The shadow root is only a styling boundary - script inside it runs in the page - and this content script can talk to the privileged worker.

outcomes.architecture: Chrome MV3 extension: a background service worker with chrome.runtime onMessage/onMessageExternal listeners, a command router, a chrome.storage.sync settings merger, fetch-based preview handlers, and content scripts that render a panel into a shadow root on every page.
outcomes.why: Every stored field is passed through `asText`, which round-trips the value through a text node so `&`, `<` and `>` come back as entities and cannot open a tag in the element content where they are used. The one value that would have had to sit in an attribute, the note id, is written through `dataset` after the markup has been parsed, and the note's CSS class can only be one of two constants from the TONE_CLASS map.

outcomes.architecture: Chrome MV3 extension: a background service worker with chrome.runtime onMessage/onMessageExternal listeners, a command router, a chrome.storage.sync settings merger, fetch-based preview handlers, and content scripts that render a panel into a shadow root on every page.
outcomes.why: `payload.url` is an href the content script read out of the page it is rendering, so it is page-controlled, and it is fetched with no parsing, no scheme check and no host restriction from a worker that holds `<all_urls>`. The status and the first 480 characters of the body are handed back to the caller, so a hostile page can use the extension to read `http://localhost` services, cloud metadata endpoints and the customer's internal wiki from inside the reader's network, past the origin policy that would otherwise stop it.

outcomes.architecture: Chrome MV3 extension: a background service worker with chrome.runtime onMessage/onMessageExternal listeners, a command router, a chrome.storage.sync settings merger, fetch-based preview handlers, and content scripts that render a panel into a shadow root on every page.
outcomes.why: `previewTarget` parses the value into a real URL first and then requires https, no embedded credentials, and a hostname that is an exact member of the closed PREVIEW_HOSTS set, returning null otherwise; the fetch uses the normalised URL and `redirect: "error"` so an allow-listed host cannot bounce the worker to an internal address. The destination is decided by the extension, not by the page.

outcomes.architecture: Socket.IO gateway plus a raw `ws` widget bridge and Express SSE routes for a support desk, over Postgres and Mongo: two sibling deployments (apps/agent-desk and apps/shared-inbox) that share the same module layout.
outcomes.why: The upgrade is completed for anyone who asks for the right path, and the identity the whole bridge then trusts is read straight off the query string: `agentId` and `orgId` are whatever the connecting client typed. No cookie, token or signature is checked anywhere in this handler, so a stranger can open `/bridge/v1?agent=...&org=<victim org>` and every frame handler downstream - which all scope their reads off `ws.session` - will serve that tenant's data.

outcomes.architecture: Socket.IO gateway plus a raw `ws` widget bridge and Express SSE routes for a support desk, over Postgres and Mongo: two sibling deployments (apps/agent-desk and apps/shared-inbox) that share the same module layout.
outcomes.why: The credential also rides on the query string, but it is a ticket the desk API minted: `verifyHandshakeTicket` recomputes the HMAC over the encoded claims with the server-side secret, compares it with `timingSafeEqual`, and rejects anything older than thirty seconds, so the agent and org on the socket are values the server asserted rather than values the client chose. A handshake without a valid ticket is answered with 401 and destroyed.

outcomes.architecture: Socket.IO gateway plus a raw `ws` widget bridge and Express SSE routes for a support desk, over Postgres and Mongo: two sibling deployments (apps/agent-desk and apps/shared-inbox) that share the same module layout.
outcomes.why: `frame.term` is client-controlled - the frame arrives as a WebSocket message and is dispatched into this handler by `routeFrame` in bridge/router.js, so the tainted value crosses a module boundary before it gets here - and it is interpolated into a quoted ILIKE literal in the statement text while the org id and limit beside it are properly bound. A quote in the search term closes the literal and the remainder is parsed as SQL, which also defeats the `m.org_id = $1` tenant predicate on the same query.

outcomes.architecture: Socket.IO gateway plus a raw `ws` widget bridge and Express SSE routes for a support desk, over Postgres and Mongo: two sibling deployments (apps/agent-desk and apps/shared-inbox) that share the same module layout.
outcomes.why: The search term is split into at most six words and each one is pushed onto `params` as its own `%word%` pattern with a matching `$n` placeholder in the clause list, so no part of the client's term ever reaches the statement text. The only interpolated fragments are the joined placeholder clauses and an ORDER BY chosen from the constant ORDERS map.

outcomes.architecture: Socket.IO gateway plus a raw `ws` widget bridge and Express SSE routes for a support desk, over Postgres and Mongo: two sibling deployments (apps/agent-desk and apps/shared-inbox) that share the same module layout.
outcomes.why: The whole client-supplied `filter` object is spread into the Mongo query, so any key and any value the agent's console sends becomes part of the selector - `{"assigneeId":{"$ne":null}}` or a `$where` clause are both accepted. Worse, the spread comes *after* `orgId` and `deletedAt`, so a filter containing `orgId` overwrites the tenant scope and reads another organisation's ticket projections, including requester names.

outcomes.architecture: Socket.IO gateway plus a raw `ws` widget bridge and Express SSE routes for a support desk, over Postgres and Mongo: two sibling deployments (apps/agent-desk and apps/shared-inbox) that share the same module layout.
outcomes.why: The view is compiled rather than merged: only keys in the FACETS allow-list survive, and every value must be a string matching an anchored character class, so no operator object can ever reach `find()`. The tenant scope and the soft-delete predicate are written after the compiled facets, which means a facet named `orgId` cannot displace them.

outcomes.architecture: Socket.IO gateway plus a raw `ws` widget bridge and Express SSE routes for a support desk, over Postgres and Mongo: two sibling deployments (apps/agent-desk and apps/shared-inbox) that share the same module layout.
outcomes.why: The authorisation is the join: the ticket row only materialises when `ticket_grants` holds a live, unrevoked grant for the socket's own agent id, which is bound as a parameter from `socket.data.session`. A ticket the caller has no grant on returns no rows and is answered with `ticket_not_found`, so the room is never joined and no panel is serialised.

outcomes.architecture: Socket.IO gateway plus a raw `ws` widget bridge and Express SSE routes for a support desk, over Postgres and Mongo: two sibling deployments (apps/agent-desk and apps/shared-inbox) that share the same module layout.
outcomes.why: The request's own `Origin` header is echoed back as `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` - falling back to `*` when absent - and paired with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. That combination lets any site the agent visits open this EventSource with the desk session cookie attached and read the tenant's live queue counters cross-origin; the reflection makes the allow-list effectively universal, and there is no `Vary: Origin` either.

outcomes.architecture: Socket.IO gateway plus a raw `ws` widget bridge and Express SSE routes for a support desk, over Postgres and Mongo: two sibling deployments (apps/agent-desk and apps/shared-inbox) that share the same module layout.
outcomes.why: The credentialed grant is only issued when the request's Origin is an exact member of the two-entry STREAM_ORIGINS set; anything else - including a request with no Origin at all - gets no CORS headers, so no third-party page can read the stream. `Vary: Origin` is set as well, so a shared cache cannot hand one shell's grant to another.

The comment above the update relies on the /approvals screen hiding the buttons, but a server function is an RPC endpoint any authenticated member can post to directly, so any employee can approve any submitted requisition in their org - including one they raised themselves.

The module's own header notes that several buyers work the same cost centre, so two orders issued together both see the same `committed_minor`, both pass the ceiling check and both commit, taking the cost centre over its budget by the smaller of the two amounts.
